source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) was tested zero-shot on text matrix problems (Digit Matrices), letter-string, four-term verbal and story analogies, against human samples. It matched or beat humans on most.
numbers: Digit Matrices: GPT-3 above human average on all types; generative OR 1.88 (p=0.005, CI 1.21-2.91); multiple choice OR 6.27 (p=2.3e-8); humans N=40. Pattern across problem subtypes correlated with humans r(30)=0.39, p=0.027.
limits: Human samples were online or college samples. Training-data overlap not ruled out (later counterfactual tests). Task is analogy, not the animal same-different or RMTS paradigm.
agent_relevance: A plain LLM shows relational induction with no scaffold. This is the baseline later work attacks.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: The Digit Matrices were built to mimic Raven's SPM rules. Human accuracy on them was very similar to SPM and showed the same pattern across problem types, so the text task taps similar rule induction.
numbers: Human SPM N=80 (earlier data); Digit Matrices humans N=40. Rule types: constant, progression, distribution-of-3, plus logic (AND, OR, XOR).
limits: SPM comparison uses different human samples; SPM15 has no three-rule problems.
agent_relevance: Gives a validated text format for testing relation induction in our agent without images.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Four-term verbal analogies: GPT-3 equalled or beat humans on the UCLA Verbal Analogy Test and the Sternberg-Nigro set, beat the estimated high-school SAT average on SAT analogies, and was numerically weaker than humans on the Jones et al. set. Like humans it did worse when A-B and C-D were semantically far apart.
numbers: Semantic-distance effect for GPT-3: OR=3.24, p=0.0165, CI 1.24-8.5. Jones et al. human N=241.
limits: Relations are common lexical ones (category, antonym, cause) that LLMs have seen often.
agent_relevance: Familiar lexical relations are cheap for the model. O7 effort belongs on novel relations.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Story analogies (Gentner materials): college students were better than GPT-3 at picking the story that shares higher-order causal relations. GPT-4 was stronger in a preliminary test.
numbers: Humans N=54; 15/54 chose the analogous story on every trial. GPT-3 vs human OR=0.37, p=0.0003, CI 0.21-0.63. Human far-analogy t(53)=16.7.
limits: GPT-4 result was preliminary, in a supplement only.
agent_relevance: Higher-order mapping is where models lagged first. This echoes the Penn et al. claim that higher-order relation use is the human-specific step.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Authors link letter-string analogies to Hofstadter and Mitchell's Copycat domain, built to study re-representation in computational models. LLMs now do the same task zero-shot without that machinery.
numbers: No Copycat accuracy figures were read.
limits: Historical context only.
agent_relevance: Older AI analogy systems used explicit mapping; the LLM route skips it, which is why the permuted-alphabet tests matter.

source: Hodel & West (2023) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Re-ran letter-string tasks with counterfactual changes (synthetic alphabet, bigger intervals). Human accuracy stayed high; GPT-3 collapsed.
numbers: GPT-3 generative accuracy on the synthetic alphabet was below 0.1 for extend-sequence, successor, predecessor and fix-alphabet. Only remove-redundant and sort stayed near the original range.
limits: GPT-3 only. The original authors disputed it.
agent_relevance: Apparent relation use partly rests on memorised alphabet order. Test any scaffold on novel symbols.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Counterfactual letter-string tasks (permuted or symbol alphabets). Humans stayed high. GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 fell on permuted alphabets and again on symbols.
numbers: Mean accuracy over all alphabets and problems: humans 0.753 (1,876 samples); GPT-3 0.488, GPT-3.5 0.350, GPT-4 0.452 (6,840 each). Counterfactual comprehension checks (successor, predecessor) were mostly near 1.0.
limits: Letter strings only. Table values read from a PDF text extract; row order assumed.
agent_relevance: The gap is in mapping, not in understanding the rule. Argues for an external check of the mapping step.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Reply to the critiques. On shuffled-alphabet letter strings plain GPT-4 was below humans, but GPT-4 with code execution matched humans.
numbers: Humans N=99 (interval 1) and N=97 (interval 2). Human vs GPT-4: P=8.9e-13. Human vs GPT-4+code: P=0.496. Correct GPT-4 answers came with accurate rule explanations; many errors followed a valid alternative rule.
quote: GPT-4 + code execution performed on par with human participants
limits: Written by the original authors. Code execution turns the task into a program, which is a scaffold more than reasoning.
agent_relevance: Direct support for our design: a program step closes the gap on symbol-mapping analogies.

source: Stevenson et al. (2024/2025) Can large language models generalize analogy solving like children can?
finding: Children (7-9), adults and LLMs solved letter-string analogies in Latin, Greek (near transfer) and symbol (far transfer) alphabets. LLMs matched children on Latin, fell on Greek, and fell much more on symbols. Children and adults transferred easily.
numbers: 42-44 children, 62 adults (6 excluded), 55 runs per LLM (Claude-3/3.5, Gemma-2 9B/27B, GPT-3/3.5/4o, Llama-3.1 405B). Five prompt templates were tried; the best was reported.
limits: Best-template reporting favours LLMs. One task family.
agent_relevance: Transfer to a new domain, not in-domain skill, is where models differ from children. Test O7 on far transfer.

source: Stevenson et al. (2024/2025)
finding: Prepending earlier solved items to each new item helped LLMs. Without it performance was generally lower. A rule-check subtask showed models applied repetition rules in new alphabets but not the ordering (successor) idea.
numbers: Best prompt: 'If A changes to B, what does C change to?'. Authors locate the failure in the abstraction of what an alphabet is (an ordered sequence), not in the analogy step.
limits: Size of the drop is in an appendix not read. Diagnosis rests on one subtask.
agent_relevance: Keep earlier solved relations in context. State the ordering relation explicitly for new symbol sets.

source: Musker et al. (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning, J. Memory and Language 145, 104676
finding: New tasks mapping words with semantic structure to letter strings and other characters. Best LLMs match humans in several conditions but react differently to word-pair order and semantic distractors.
numbers: Permuting pair order lowered LLM accuracy but not humans: Claude 3 coef -1.78 (z=-4.22), GPT-4 -1.68 (z=-3.98), Llama-405B -2.34 (z=-5.50), all p<0.001. Study 2: best LLM matched humans in all conditions and exceeded them in compositional variants.
limits: Authors conclude LLMs give a how-possibly but not how-actually account of human analogy.
agent_relevance: Order sensitivity argues for restating or shuffling inputs as a cheap test.

source: Hu et al. (2023) In-context analogical reasoning with pre-trained language models
finding: Text-encoded Raven's matrices given zero-shot. Naming attributes with ordinal numeric symbols beat image-like and random-name encodings. Splitting the problem by attribute helped more.
numbers: Quasi-image and random-naming encodings reached at most 28.2% and 51.8%. Decomposition added 2.8 points for GPT-3 175B; OPT 125M rose from 22.2% to 45.6%. Ordinal naming beat random naming by over 20 points in larger models. Supervised Rel-AIR and CoPINet+ACL were baselines.
limits: Perfect perception assumed. No human data.
agent_relevance: How a relation is named in the prompt moves accuracy by tens of points. A direct O7 lever.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (ICLR)
finding: Analogical prompting: the model writes its own related example problems, then solves the target. A method from analogy research used inside a prompt. It beat 0-shot CoT and few-shot CoT.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-3.5-turbo: 0-shot 75.0, 0-shot CoT 75.8, 5-shot CoT 76.7, ours 77.8%. text-davinci-003: 14.8/50.3/54.0/61.0%. PaLM2: 60.8/78.2/80.7/81.7%. MATH GPT-3.5: 33.0/33.9/34.9/37.3%. Codeforces GPT-4 Acc@1/Acc@10: 3-shot CoT 17/31%, knowledge+exemplars 19/37%.
limits: Small gains on strong models. Of 50 failures, 10 had irrelevant exemplars and 12 had wrong ones; 28 had correct exemplars but still failed.
agent_relevance: Cheapest relational method to drop into an agent loop. Gains are largest on weaker models.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Reasoning or reciting? Counterfactual tasks
finding: 11 default-versus-counterfactual task pairs (base-9 arithmetic, shifted chess, new tunings, SET variants). All models did worse on the counterfactual twin, sometimes near-perfect to near-zero, but above chance.
numbers: Arithmetic dropped from near-perfect to near-zero in some counterfactual settings. Counterfactual comprehension checks separated misreading from real failure.
limits: Not analogy-specific. It is the source of the counterfactual method used by the letter-string critics.
agent_relevance: A reusable test for any O7 step: swap the surface rules and see if the step still works.

source: Gendron et al. (2023) Large language models are not strong abstract reasoners
finding: Benchmark of abstract tasks (ACRE text and symbolic, Evals-P, RAVEN text). LLMs scored low. Scores were higher in symbolic than in natural-language form. Chain of thought did not rescue them.
numbers: Multiple choice, ACRE text vs symbolic: GPT-4 0.272 vs 0.512; GPT-3.5-Turbo 0.184 vs 0.445; text-davinci-003 0.098 vs 0.427 (random listed 0.33). RAVEN-text GPT-4 0.535.
limits: Columns read from a text extract; random baselines differ by task.
agent_relevance: Natural-language wrapping hurts relational tasks. Strip to symbols when the relation is the point.

source: Gendron et al. (2023)
finding: Chain-of-thought versions were often no better than base prompts; GPT-4's lead over GPT-3.5 shrank under CoT. Models overfit to some causal path types on the text version only.
numbers: CoT results slightly lower than base for some models; no large drop.
limits: Authors propose guiding generation along causal paths; untested here.
agent_relevance: Plain CoT is not an O7 fix for relations.

source: Yiu et al. (2025) KiVA: Kid-inspired visual analogies for large multimodal models (ICLR)
finding: 4,300 visual transformations of everyday objects, compared with children aged 3-5 and adults. Models name WHAT changed but fail at HOW MUCH and at applying the rule to new objects.
numbers: Three stages: classification (chance 25%), specification and extrapolation (chance 33%). GPT-o1, GPT-4V, LLaVA-1.5, MANTIS tested. GPT-o1, GPT-4V and MANTIS beat children only on rotation and color classification.
limits: Children's data cover a subset; adult set is larger.
agent_relevance: Noticing a relation is easy for models; quantifying and transferring it is not. Same split as in animal work (noticing vs using).

source: Tartaglini et al. (2023) Deep neural networks can learn generalizable same-different visual relations
finding: Earlier work said CNNs cannot learn same-different, the task used with baboons, pigeons and crows. Fine-tuned CLIP-pretrained ViTs can, including out of distribution.
numbers: CLIP ViT-B/16 fine-tuned on Squiggles: >95% median test accuracy on all three OOD sets; up to 90% on a photorealistic 3D set with no fine-tuning there; nearly 100% in-distribution. Median of five seeds.
limits: ViTs favour colour and texture over shape unless the data lack those cues. ViT-B/16 beats ResNet-50 after pretraining.
agent_relevance: Relational ability depends on pretraining diversity, not special machinery.

source: Geiger, Carstensen, Frank, Potts (2022) Relational reasoning and generalization using non-symbolic neural networks
finding: Revisits the claim that networks cannot learn equality. With pretrained or random input representations, networks learned identity, ABA sequence patterns from positive examples only, and a hierarchical equality task zero-shot.
numbers: Means over 20 runs; vocabulary 20 for the ABA task; hidden sizes 2-100 compared.
limits: Results depend on input representation and number of training examples. Numbers read from figures only.
agent_relevance: Counters the symbols-are-required view; supports using plain models for O7.

source: Webb, Sinha, Cohen (2021) Emergent symbols through binding in external memory (ICLR)
finding: ESBN, a recurrent net with external memory for variable binding, generalizes same/different, relational match-to-sample (RMTS), distribution-of-three and identity rules to unseen items.
numbers: Over 95% test accuracy in all four tasks, with as few as two training entities (same/different). Same/different with m=98 of 100 items held out: ESBN+TCN 100.0; plain Transformer 56.1; LSTM 56.5; RN 52.3. ESBN without TCN stayed at 50.0.
limits: Design detail (TCN) matters: ESBN alone failed.
agent_relevance: RMTS solved by explicit binding. A scaffold can imitate this by passing role labels in the prompt.

source: Altabaa, Webb, Lafferty (2024) Abstractors and relational cross-attention (ICLR)
finding: A Transformer module that separates relations from object features. Better sample efficiency on relational sequence tasks and more robust to noise on held-out objects than standard Transformers.
numbers: Evaluated on discriminative relational tasks, sorting seq-to-seq tasks and math problem solving; robustness tested at several noise levels, 5 trials each.
limits: Architecture change; needs training.
agent_relevance: The gap can be closed by design; for a scaffold the principle is to keep relation separate from content.

source: Monk, Meyer, Ngo (2024) Large language models and relational match-to-sample (preprint 202401.1681)
finding: From a search snippet only: language models tested on relational match-to-sample failed, though humans pass it and some animals do.
numbers: Not read. Page returned HTTP 403 and the PDF download failed. No numbers verified.
limits: Unverified preprint. Models tested and dates unknown.
agent_relevance: Most on-topic LLM study found. Verify before use.
